content:
Hi all, I have the following example with a working and non-working case at the very end:

import Mathlib

namespace Bin
inductive Bit : Type
| zero : Bit
| one : Bit
deriving DecidableEq
abbrev Binary := List Bit
end Bin

namespace Bool
def Binary (C : ℕ) : Type := { enc : Bin.Binary // List.length enc = C }
end Bool

def rr₀ (y x: Bool.Binary C) : ℚ := sorry

structure Binary (C : ℕ) (W : Bin.Binary → ℕ) where
  val : Bool.Binary C
instance : CoeOut (Binary C W) (Bool.Binary C) := ⟨fun x => x.val⟩

def explicit_type_coersion_works (x: Binary C W) : rr₀ x (x : Bool.Binary C) = 0 := sorry
def implicit_type_coersion_does_not_work (x: Binary C W) : rr₀ x x = 0 := sorry

and if you try it on the playground the second line will produce and error like

Application type mismatch: The argument
  x
has type
  Binary C W
but is expected to have type
  Bool.Binary ?m.3
in the application
  rr₀ ?m.4 x

and it seems the C of the rr-expected type was overshadowed as a metavariable m.3. Why do we need the explicit type specification as in the first case and Lean 4 cannot pick the C from the CoeOut instance we have already specified?
Perhaps this is some important detail about the order of type resolution and auto-coercion steps that would somehow end up not performing the provided auto-coercion on time?
I think since it still has metavariables finding the coercion is postponed

To simplify the above reproducer even further, considering the background context:

import Mathlib

namespace Bin
inductive Bit : Type
| zero : Bit
| one : Bit
deriving DecidableEq
abbrev Binary := List Bit
end Bin

namespace Bool
def Binary (C : ℕ) : Type := { enc : Bin.Binary // List.length enc = C }
end Bool

structure Binary (C : ℕ) (W : Bin.Binary → ℕ) where
  val : Bool.Binary C
instance : CoeOut (Binary C W) (Bool.Binary C) := ⟨fun x => x.val⟩

the original example mentioned inability to perform implicit coercion of x in

def q₂ (y x: Bool.Binary C) : ℚ := sorry

-- explicit coercion works
def explicit_type_coersion_works (y x: Binary C W) : q₂ y (x : Bool.Binary C) = 0 := sorry
-- implicit coercion doesn't work:
/-
Application type mismatch: The argument
  x
has type
  Binary C W
but is expected to have type
  Bool.Binary ?m.3
in the application
  rr₀ ?m.4 x
-/
def implicit_type_coersion_does_not_work (y x: Binary C W) : q₂ y x = 0 := sorry

Note that the working case only needs one argument (the second one) to be coerced and works without coercing the first so I guess Lean needs a more coherent one-time way of being informed about the type.

A second interesting example involves use of global variables like:

variable (x : Binary C W)
def q (x : Bool.Binary C) : ℚ := sorry

-- using the expected type in a definition-local variable works
def ex1 (x : Bool.Binary C) : Prop := q x = 1
-- explicit coercion works
def ex2 : Prop := q (x : Bool.Binary C) = 1
-- implicit coercion of the defined variable doesn't work:
/-
Application type mismatch: The argument
  x
has type
  Binary C W
but is expected to have type
  Bool.Binary ?m.3
in the application
  q x
-/
def ex3 : Prop := q x = 1

Looks like this works with Coe. Seems like problems is caused by CoeOut?

import Lean

variable (x : Int)
def q (x : Lean.Json) : Nat := sorry

-- using the expected type in a definition-local variable works
def ex1 (x : Lean.Json) : Prop := q x = 1
-- explicit coercion works
def ex2 : Prop := q (x : Lean.Json) = 1
-- implicit coercion of the defined variable doesn't work:
/-
Application type mismatch: The argument
  x
has type
  Binary C W
but is expected to have type
  Bool.Binary ?m.3
in the application
  q x
-/
def ex3 := q x = 1

Jakub Nowak said:

def q (x : Lean.Json) : Nat := sorry

I think you need a more elaborate type with one or two type parameters in order to reproduce this on your side. Let me know if you know about any such types from the standard library or Mathlib.

Here is an even simpler reproducer than everything above that demonstrates that CoeOut works fine when removing one type parameter to zero type parameters but not when removing two type parameters down to one type parameter:

import Mathlib

def nc (C : ℕ) : Type := { a : List ℕ // List.length a = C }
structure ncw (C W : ℕ) where
  val : nc C

instance : CoeOut (nc C) (List ℕ) := ⟨fun x => x.val⟩
instance : CoeOut (ncw C W) (nc C) := ⟨fun x => x.val⟩

def f1 (_ : List ℕ) : ℕ := 0
def f2 (_ : nc C) : ℕ := 0

-- implicit coercion works with CoeOut and just one parameter
def ex11 (x : nc C) : Prop := f1 x = 1
-- implicit coercion of the defined variable doesn't work:
/-
Application type mismatch: The argument
  x
has type
  ncw C W
but is expected to have type
  nc ?m.3
in the application
  f x
-/
def ex21 (x : ncw C W) : Prop := f2 x = 1
-- explicit coercion works
def ex22 (x : ncw C W) : Prop := f2 (x : nc C) = 1
Check #mwe, you forgot import Mathlib. But otherwise, that's a very good mwe, gj.

Indeed, I was copying from the Lean web compiler to validate everything but had another block I wanted to skip to make this reproducer minimal. Thanks for catching this with a good reference, corrected via edit.

Is this something worth reporting as an issue or is this limitation by design for some reason?

Looks like no one here can answer. I think you should create an issue. This is a limitation, so it should either be fixed, or documented (which doesn't seem to be, at least I couldn't find anything). Though, it's probably a limitation of class synthesis, so unlikely it will be fixed.

Instance synthesis can't find CoeOut (ncw C W) (nc C) instance: 

import Mathlib

def nc (C : ℕ) : Type := { a : List ℕ // List.length a = C }
structure ncw (C W : ℕ) where
  val : nc C

instance : CoeOut (nc C) (List ℕ) := ⟨fun x => x.val⟩
instance : CoeOut (ncw C W) (nc C) := ⟨fun x => x.val⟩

def f1 (_ : List ℕ) : ℕ := 0
def f2 (_ : nc C) : ℕ := 0

/--
error: typeclass instance problem is stuck, it is often due to metavariables
  CoeOut (ncw C W) (nc ?m.3)
-/
#guard_msgs in
example (x : ncw C W) : Prop := f2 (CoeOut.coe x) = 1
If this is a technical question about mathlib then you could ask it in #mathlib4 , many experts are not reading this channel which is typically full of beginner questions

The problem here is that coercions (or instance search in general) can't assign metavariables (but this is intentional). Take this as an example:

-- ...
instance : CoeOut (Binary C W) (Bool.Binary C) := ⟨fun x => x.val⟩
instance : CoeOut (Bool.Binary C) (Bool.Binary 4) := ⟨fun _ => ⟨[.zero, .zero, .zero, .zero], rfl⟩⟩

def explicit_type_coersion_works (x: Binary C W) : rr₀ x (x : Bool.Binary C) = 0 := sorry
def explicit_type_coersion_works' (x: Binary C W) : rr₀ x (x : Bool.Binary 4) = 0 := sorry

If coercions were able to just assign metavariables, then in the second example, it would see that we want a coercion Binary C W => Bool.Binary ?C for the first parameter and just assign ?C := C; but then we later need ?C := 4! So coercion elaboration is postponed until it can know for sure what to coerce to; which in the case of the implicit coercion is, well, never.

Of course, in your example, there is no second coercion instance that could cause trouble; but instance synthesis (of the CoeT (Binary C W) x (Bool.Binary _) instance) isn't smart enough to figure that out.

Kevin Buzzard said:

If this is a technical question about mathlib then you could ask it in #mathlib4 , many experts are not reading this channel which is typically full of beginner questions

Indeed, the problem is that sometimes I (and maybe other people around here) are not sure if a question is an actual issue or perhaps a beginners question about something simple we may not be understanding upon discovery or have a blind spot on. I assume it is not easy to move a conversation across channels on tulip.

The problem here is that coercions (or instance search in general) can't assign metavariables (but this is intentional).

Maybe this could instead be a default behavior that could somehow be overridden just like we can override other behaviors when we somehow signal to the elaborator that we know what we are doing?

Robin Arnez said:

Of course, in your example, there is no second coercion instance that could cause trouble; but instance synthesis (of the CoeT (Binary C W) x (Bool.Binary _) instance) isn't smart enough to figure that out.

Perhaps a fine-tuned version of this elaboration could only postpone variable assignment if it finds conflicts or better yet indicate such conflicts back to the user via proper error messages. Even having multiple ambiguous coercion paths between two types that don't commute or bring to the same type parameters could be considered as a related error.

I think that's kinda what marking parameter as outParam/semiOutParam does? It is saying to instance finder that it can use instances of that class even if that parameter contains metavariables. But this mechanism cannot be used here. Maybe a mechanism to mark a specific variable on an individual instance as out/semi-out is something that could be added to the language?
